prompt: A continuous function $P(t)$ models the population (in thousands) of a town, where $t$ is years after 2000. Records show $P(0) = 12$, $P(10) = 20$ and $P(20) = 15$. What is the MINIMUM number of times in the interval $[0, 20]$ that the population must have been exactly $17$ thousand?
hint: Apply the Intermediate Value Theorem on each stretch separately: $[0, 10]$ and $[10, 20]$.

hints.text: Apply the Intermediate Value Theorem on each stretch separately: $[0, 10]$ and $[10, 20]$.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: a continuous function with $f(0) = 1$ and $f(5) = 3$ must hit $2$ at least once on $[0, 5]$. Now count how many stretches here have $17$ trapped between the endpoint values.
On $[0, 10]$ the population goes $12 \to 20$: is $17$ in between? On $[10, 20]$ it goes $20 \to 15$: is $17$ in between?
Yes on both stretches, so the population was exactly $17$ thousand at least once going up and at least once coming down: minimum $2$ times.

explanation: On $[0, 10]$: $P$ is continuous and $12 < 17 < 20$, so by the IVT there is a time with $P = 17$.
On $[10, 20]$: $15 < 17 < 20$, so there is another such time, and it is different because it lies in a different stretch (at $t = 10$ itself $P = 20 \ne 17$).
The IVT guarantees at least one crossing on each stretch, so the minimum is $2$. The real number could be larger if the population wobbled.

alternativeExplanations.title: Draw the dots and connect them
steps: Plot $(0, 12)$, $(10, 20)$ and $(20, 15)$, then draw the horizontal line at height $17$.
Any continuous curve through the three dots must cross that line on the way up and again on the way down.
Two crossings are forced; a wiggly curve could cross more, but never fewer.
